draft:
An unpredictable schedule is a system for transferring risk. The employer gets labour when demand appears; you get the empty hours, cancelled plans, missed appointments, and frantic rearrangements when it doesn’t. Calling this a scheduling inconvenience is like calling a pickpocket an awkward hug. The defining fact isn’t that the software makes mistakes. It’s that every mistake becomes your emergency.

A scheduling vendor may call the system “optimization” (the polite word for squeezing slack out of somebody else’s life). From the employer’s side, an unfilled hour looks like waste. From your side, that same hour might be the margin that lets you collect a child, attend a class, sleep properly, or work a second job. The software treats that margin as idle capacity because it can’t see the life attached to it.

What happens when your shift changes six hours before it begins? You absorb the cost. You find transport, negotiate care, abandon other work, or lose the wages. The dashboard records a clean adjustment; your household records a small crisis. That asymmetry – one party clicks while another party scrambles – is the mechanism, not a side effect.

I think we should call this what it is: control over time. Wages purchase specified hours of labour. Short-notice scheduling reaches beyond those hours and places a soft claim on the rest (usually without paying for it). If you must remain ready because a shift might appear, that readiness has value. If refusing the shift threatens future hours, the choice isn’t free merely because the screen includes a button marked “decline.”

Employers do face real uncertainty. A rush may arrive; a delivery may be late; someone may call in sick. Software can help match people to work, and organisers shouldn’t pretend every schedule can be carved in stone. But uncertainty doesn’t vanish when management exports it. It lands on workers – in smaller paycheques, broken routines, and hours spent waiting – while the firm keeps the benefit of flexibility.

I call that arrangement a rigged game. The house changes the start time after you’ve placed your bet, then congratulates itself for running an efficient table. You’re expected to treat availability as limitless, but the employer’s obligations remain precisely bounded. “Flexibility” flows one way. That’s bullshit, and the software makes it scalable.

I mean scalable in a precise sense. A manager can be unfair to a dozen people; an automated scheduler can impose the same unfair rule across a workforce while presenting each disruption as an isolated recommendation (and therefore nobody’s decision). The machine supplies distance, not innocence. We still have to ask who chose the objective, whose costs entered the calculation, and whose costs disappeared.

My test is simple: does the system give workers power equal to the burden it creates? Advance notice, consent, predictable minimum hours, extra pay for late changes, and protection against retaliation all convert “flexibility” from a command into a bargain. Workers also need access to schedule records (including changes and cancellations), because a pattern that stays hidden on individual phones is harder to contest together.

Labour organisers can make the invisible claim on time visible. Compare notices, log changes, calculate the unpaid disruption, and bargain over the rule rather than each alert. We shouldn’t accept a system that reserves your life for the employer while buying only the fragments it uses. Unpredictability isn’t merely an inconvenience imposed by software. It is power exercised through software, and our demand should be equally plain: if employers want control of workers’ time, they must negotiate for it and pay for it.
